content: Zaspopathy, also known as ZASP-related myofibril myopathy, is a recently identified autosomal dominant form of progressive muscular dystrophy. It was first described in the medical literature in 2005. This condition encompasses a spectrum of myopathies that can affect both distal and proximal muscle groups. The underlying cause of zaspopathy is mutations in the ZASP gene. The ZASP gene is located on chromosome 10 and encodes a protein that is associated with the Z-disk, a critical structural component of the contractile apparatus in muscle cells. Mutations in the ZASP protein lead to the disintegration of the Z-disk within the myofibrils, which are the contractile elements of muscle cells. This structural disruption impairs the integrity and function of muscle fibers, contributing to the progressive muscle weakness observed in affected individuals. Additionally, mutations in other Z-disk-associated proteins, such as desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, and myotilin, can result in disorders that share clinical and pathological similarities with zaspopathy. These related conditions highlight the critical role of Z-disk proteins in maintaining the structural and functional integrity of muscle tissue.
